# Thyrowise -- Thyroid Tracker for Hashimoto's and Hypothyroidism
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/

Thyrowise

A thyroid tracker that keeps everything on your phone.

Thyrowise logs your TSH, your levothyroxine doses and the symptoms
that drift in between -- with no account, no login and no server to leak.
It is free on iPhone and Apple Watch.

Get Thyrowise on the App Store

Free to download * iPhone and Apple Watch * 11 languages * Android in progress

What it does

Living with hypothyroidism or Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a small pill every
morning, labs every few months, and symptoms that move slowly enough to be hard
to remember by the next appointment. Thyrowise holds those three things in one
place.

Labs. Log TSH, free T4, free T3, total T4, total T3, TPO
antibodies and thyroglobulin antibodies, with the date each was drawn.

Medication. A daily levothyroxine reminder that, once you
mark the dose taken, counts down the empty-stomach wait and then tells you
coffee and breakfast are fine.

Dose changes. Record what your doctor changed and when, so
the next lab result has something to be read against.

Symptoms. One-tap chips for fatigue, brain fog, hair loss,
cold intolerance and the rest.

Nodules and scans. Store what the ultrasound report said,
including its TI-RADS category, and follow a nodule's measurements over time.

The part people notice first

Levothyroxine is absorbed best on an empty stomach, so most people take it
first thing and wait 30 to 60 minutes before coffee or
breakfast. Thyrowise runs that wait as a live countdown on the Lock Screen and
on the Apple Watch, so you are not guessing whether enough time has passed.

Source: Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information, U.S. National Library of Medicine.

No account, and nothing to leak

Thyrowise has no sign-up, no login and no server. Every lab value, dose and
symptom is written to your own device and stays there. There is no analytics SDK
and no advertising SDK in the app, so there is no profile of your thyroid disease
sitting anywhere to be breached, sold, or lost when a company shuts down.

The practical consequence: nobody can lock you out of your own history, and
export is a plain PDF or CSV you own.

What the phone already knows

Weight, sleep and resting heart rate are three of the things people with an
under- or over-treated thyroid actually watch, and an iPhone or Apple Watch is
already measuring them. If you turn it on, Thyrowise reads those from Apple Health
and shows them beside your log, so the picture is not limited to what you
remembered to tap.

Nothing is inferred or diagnosed from them. The read is optional, off until you
enable it, and can be revoked in Health at any time.

What is free and what is paid

| Free, permanently | Thyrowise Pro

| Unlimited lab logging -- TSH, free T4, free T3, TPO antibodies
| TSH trend chart against your own target band, with dose changes marked

| One-tap symptom logging
| Dose impact -- symptoms and TSH before vs after an adjustment

| Daily medication reminders with the absorption countdown
| Symptom trends -- the last 30 days against the 30 before

| Dose-change log and full history, on device
| Endocrinologist-ready PDF and CSV export

Pro is 9.99 USD monthly, 29.99 USD yearly with a 7-day free trial, or 59.99 USD
once for a lifetime unlock. The free tier is not a trial and does not expire.

Every medical statement in the app is sourced

Thyrowise does not generate advice. Where it states a number -- a typical
reference range, a retest interval, an absorption rule -- it names the published
source, and a Sources screen in the app lists all of them. Those sources are the
American Thyroid Association,
NIDDK at the National Institutes of Health,
MedlinePlus at the U.S. National Library of
Medicine, and the American College of Radiology for TI-RADS.

Insights in the app are counts of your own logs, stated as counts. There is no
score, no risk model and no black-box AI making a guess about your thyroid.

Read next

How long to wait after levothyroxine before coffee

Frequently asked questions

Thyrowise is a tracking and reminder tool. It is not a medical device and does
not give medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Reference ranges are
approximate and vary between laboratories. Always follow your doctor's plan;
never change your dose based on the app.

# Best Thyroid Tracker Apps: How to Choose, and Where Thyrowise Falls Short
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/best-thyroid-tracker-apps/

Thyrowise

How to choose a thyroid tracker app: 7 things that actually matter.

Most thyroid apps look alike on the store page. These are the
differences that decide whether you still have your data in three years.

1. Where does the data live?

This is the first question, not the last one. An app with an account keeps your
thyroid history on someone else's server, which means a company failure, a policy
change or a breach is a thing that can happen to your medical record. An app that
stores on-device cannot lose your data to any of those -- but it also cannot get it
back for you if you lose the phone without a backup.

Neither answer is wrong. Choosing without knowing which one you picked is.

2. Does it hold your target range, or a generic one?

A typical adult TSH reference range is about 0.4-4.0 mIU/L, but plenty of
people on levothyroxine are being steered to a narrower target. An app that
colours everything under 4.0 as "normal" is useless to someone told to stay under
2.5. Look for a personal band you can set yourself.
More on ranges and why labs disagree.

3. Are dose changes first-class objects?

A TSH value on its own says very little. A TSH value six weeks after a dose
went from 75 to 88 micrograms says something. If dose changes are just free text
in a notes field, the app cannot line them up against results -- and the single
most useful view, the trend with changes marked on it, is impossible.

4. How long does a normal day take?

Daily logging is only sustained if it costs seconds. One-tap symptom chips get
kept; a form with sliders and a free-text box gets abandoned in a month, and one
abandoned month is most of the value gone when the review interval is six.

5. Can you get the data out?

PDF for the appointment, CSV for yourself. Export is also your exit: an app you
can leave is an app you can safely commit to. If there is no export, every entry
you make increases the cost of ever switching.

6. Does it cite anything?

Any app stating a reference range, a retest interval or an absorption rule is
making a medical claim. Check whether it says where the claim came from. Named
sources -- the American Thyroid Association,
NIDDK,
MedlinePlus -- mean someone did the work and
you can check it. No sources means you are trusting a developer's memory.

7. Does it tell you things, or guess at them?

"Fatigue on 19 of the last 30 days, against 8 in the 30 before" is a count you
can verify and take to a doctor. A wellness score out of 100, or an AI paragraph
about what your labs suggest, is a black box in a domain where the treatment
decision is not yours to make. Prefer the count.

Where Thyrowise fits -- and where it does not

Thyrowise is built to a specific shape: private, single-device, one person,
sourced, no guessing. That makes it a poor fit for several perfectly reasonable
wants.

| Thyrowise does | Thyrowise does not

| Work with no account and no server, everything on device | Sync automatically across devices -- the backup is a JSON file you save and restore yourself

| Chart TSH against the band your doctor gave you | Offer a patient community or peer support

| Treat dose changes as dated events on the same timeline | Run on Android -- that version is still in progress

| Count the empty-stomach wait down on the Lock Screen and Watch | Provide meal plans, recipes or supplement programmes

| Export an endocrinologist-ready PDF and a CSV | Import lab results automatically from a hospital portal

| Name a published source for every medical statement | Interpret your labs, score you, or suggest a dose

Other apps in this category

Listed so this page is useful rather than only promotional. Each description
is drawn from the app's own store listing or website; features change, so check
before you commit.

ThyForLife -- tracking combined
with a global thyroid community platform, iOS and Android.

Thyra --
thyroid symptom tracking.

Papillon -- Thyroid Lab Tracker
-- lab-result logging, describes data as stored locally on the phone,
Android.

HashiTrack
-- Hashimoto's symptom and trigger tracking with AI-generated insights,
Android.

Hashimoto's Journey
-- medication adherence and lab logging.

CareClinic -- a
general health tracker with thyroid and TSH support.

Last checked September 2026.

# Thyrowise FAQ -- Privacy, Pricing, Android, Apple Watch
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/faq/

Thyrowise

Frequently asked questions.

Short answers. If yours is not here, email
aykutaydmr@gmail.com and a person will reply.

Is Thyrowise free?

Yes, and the free tier is not a trial. Logging labs, symptoms, doses and
medication reminders stays free. Thyrowise Pro is optional --
9.99 USD monthly, 29.99 USD yearly with a 7-day free trial, or 59.99 USD once for
a lifetime unlock -- and adds the TSH trend chart against your own band,
dose-impact comparison, symptom trends, the endocrinologist-ready PDF and CSV
export.

Does it need an account?

No. No sign-up, no login, no server. There is no account to be locked out of,
and no database of your thyroid history anywhere to be breached.

Does it work offline?

Entirely. The app never needs a connection to log or read anything.

Where is my data stored?

On your device. A backup is a plain, readable JSON file that you export and put
wherever you like -- Files, your own iCloud Drive, a Mac. It is readable rather
than an opaque blob on purpose: a backup you cannot open is a promise you cannot
check.

What if I lose my phone?

The honest answer: with no server, a lost phone is a lost history unless you
exported a backup first. Restoring replaces what is in the app rather
than merging, and it says so before it does it.

Is there an Android version?

Not yet -- iPhone and Apple Watch today, Android in progress.

Is there an Apple Watch app?

Yes. Mark the dose taken from the wrist; the empty-stomach countdown runs there
and on the Lock Screen.

Does it connect to Apple Health?

If you turn it on. Thyrowise can read weight, sleep, steps and resting heart
rate and show them beside your log. Off by default, revocable in Health, and
nothing is inferred or diagnosed from it.

Which lab values can I track?

TSH, free T4, free T3, total T4, total T3, TPO antibodies, thyroglobulin
antibodies and reverse T3 -- each with the date drawn. Thyroid nodules and
ultrasound scans too, including the TI-RADS category from the report.

Can I get my data out?

PDF for the appointment, CSV for yourself, JSON for a full backup.

Does it tell me what my results mean?

No, and that is deliberate. Insights are counts of your own logs -- "fatigue on
19 of the last 30 days, against 8 in the 30 before". Every medical statement in
the app names its source, and the app lists them all on a Sources screen.
What the ranges are and where they come from.

What languages does it support?

Eleven: English, Spanish, Simplified Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Brazilian
Portuguese, French, German, Japanese, Russian and Turkish.

Does it work for hyperthyroidism or Graves'?

Partly. Lab logging, symptoms and the trend chart apply to any thyroid
condition. The medication side is built around a daily levothyroxine dose and its
empty-stomach wait, so it fits hypothyroidism and Hashimoto's best.

How do I cancel Pro?

In your Apple ID settings, any time -- at least 24 hours before the period ends
to avoid renewal. Lifetime is one-time and has nothing to cancel.

Get Thyrowise on the App Store

Free * iPhone and Apple Watch * no account, no server

Thyrowise is a tracking and reminder tool. It is not a medical device and does
not give medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Reference ranges are
approximate and vary between laboratories. Always follow your doctor's plan;
never change your dose based on the app.

# Tracking Hashimoto's Symptoms So the Appointment Is Worth Something
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/hashimotos-symptom-tracking/

Thyrowise

Tracking Hashimoto's symptoms so the appointment is worth something.

Fifteen minutes, twice a year, and the honest answer to "how have
you been feeling?" is usually "fine, I think". A log turns that into a pattern
your doctor can actually use.

The problem with remembering

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid, and
what makes it hard to describe is the timescale. Symptoms move over weeks and
months, not hours. By the appointment you are reporting how the last three days
went, weighted by how today is going -- which is not the question being asked.

Background: Hashimoto's Thyroiditis, American Thyroid Association; Hashimoto's Disease, NIDDK.

What is worth logging

The symptoms commonly associated with an underactive thyroid are the ones to
start from: fatigue, brain fog, cold intolerance, hair loss, dry skin, weight
change, constipation, low mood, muscle aches.

Source: Hypothyroidism, American Thyroid Association; Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid), NIDDK.

Pick four or five of them, not all of them. A short list gets
kept for a year; a long one gets abandoned in three weeks, and three weeks of
data is worth nothing when the interval that matters is six months.

How often, and how much detail

Daily, and almost no detail. A one-tap mark beats a paragraph, because the
thing you are building is a series -- and a series survives only if logging costs
you five seconds on a bad day. Detail is for the days when something unusual
happens: a missed dose, a new supplement, a week of illness.

Log these too, or the symptoms mean less

Dose changes -- with the date. Without them, a symptom
trend has no cause to be lined up against.

Lab results -- with the date drawn, not the date you were
told.

New medications and supplements -- particularly calcium,
iron and magnesium, which block levothyroxine absorption and need at least
four hours of separation.

What not to bother tracking

TPO antibodies. They are the marker associated with Hashimoto's and are usually
measured once, to answer a diagnostic question -- following the number over time
does not track how the thyroid is doing. The same goes for thyroglobulin
antibodies, which are reported against each laboratory's own cut-off rather than
one shared number.

Sources: ATA, NIDDK, MedlinePlus.

Arriving with something readable

An endocrinologist has minutes, not an evening. What lands is one page: the TSH
series with dose changes marked on it, and the symptom counts for the period
either side of each change. Not a diary. Not a screenshot of an app you have to
explain first.

The question that page answers is the only one worth the appointment: after the
last adjustment, did anything actually change?

What Thyrowise does about it

Symptoms are one-tap chips on the home screen. Labs, doses and dose changes
share the same timeline. Pro turns all of it into a one-tap PDF built for handing
across a desk, plus a CSV if you would rather keep your own copy.

The insights are counts of your own logs, stated as counts -- "fatigue on 19 of
the last 30 days, against 8 in the 30 before". No score, no AI guess about what it
means. What it means is a conversation with your doctor.

Get Thyrowise on the App Store

Free * iPhone and Apple Watch * no account, no server

About this page

Written by the developer of Thyrowise. I am not a doctor and this is
not medical advice -- it is a plain-language write-up of published

and check.

approximate and vary between laboratories. Always follow your doctor's plan;
never change your dose based on the app.

# How Long to Wait After Levothyroxine Before Coffee
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/levothyroxine-coffee-timing/

Thyrowise

How long to wait after levothyroxine before coffee?

Take it on an empty stomach and wait 30 to 60 minutes before
breakfast or coffee. Keep calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids at least four
hours away.

The short answer

Food: 30 to 60 minutes. Coffee: an hour. Levothyroxine is
absorbed best on an empty stomach, so it is taken first thing and breakfast is
held back. Coffee is given its own, longer interval because it interferes with
absorption directly rather than merely breaking the fast.

Calcium and iron supplements: 2 to 4 hours, and they are the
ones people most often get wrong.

Sources: Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information, U.S. National Library of Medicine; Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements -- A Systematic Review.

Why coffee gets its own rule

Coffee is not just the first thing that breaks the fast. It interferes with
levothyroxine specifically, and the effect has been measured.

In the study that established this, espresso swallowed together with the
tablet lowered the rise in serum T4 by 36% on average in thyroid patients
and 29% in healthy volunteers, with peak levels down 30% and 19%. The
proposed mechanism is that coffee sequesters the hormone in the gut, leaving less
of it available to be taken up.

Sources: Benvenga S et al., Altered intestinal absorption of L-thyroxine caused by coffee, Thyroid 2008;18(3):293-301; figures as reported in Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements -- A Systematic Review.

That is why the guidance for coffee is an hour, not the 30
minutes that is often enough for food. The same review notes that liquid
levothyroxine formulations did not show a significant interaction with coffee --
if the hour is genuinely impossible for you, that is a question worth putting to
your doctor rather than something to solve on your own.

The four-hour rule is a different rule

Some things need much more separation than breakfast does. Keep
calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids at least 4 hours away from
a levothyroxine dose -- they block absorption rather than merely slowing it.

Source: Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information, U.S. National Library of Medicine.

This is the one people get wrong most often, because a calcium or iron
supplement feels like part of the same morning routine as the thyroid tablet. If
both are daily, the usual fix is to move the supplement to the evening.

Consistency beats precision

The dose you are on was arrived at by measuring your TSH some weeks after a
change -- usually 6 to 12 weeks after -- while you were taking the
tablet in whatever way you take it.

Source: Hypothyroidism, American Thyroid Association.

That means a routine you can actually keep is worth more than an ideal one you
follow twice a week. If 60 minutes without coffee is not going to survive a
Tuesday, a reliable 30 is the better answer -- and if you take it at night
instead, well after your last meal, that is a routine too. The failure mode is
not "wrong window", it is a different window every day, because then a TSH result
has nothing stable to be read against.

The trap nobody warns you about: the morning drink

The calcium tablet is easy to spot. The thing that actually catches people is
breakfast in a carton -- a meal-replacement, protein or fibre drink taken on the
way out the door, at exactly the wrong moment.

The reason is simpler than a special interaction: it is food, and it is
arriving at the exact moment the tablet needs an empty stomach. On top of that,
MedlinePlus names soybeans, walnuts and dietary fibre as things
that can affect how levothyroxine works for you -- so a carton with added fibre
or soy protein is doing more than just breaking the fast.

Milk as food is a smaller problem than a calcium tablet

These are two different sizes of the same effect, and it is worth keeping
them apart.

Calcium and iron supplements need 2 to 4 hours of
separation; MedlinePlus gives at least 4 for calcium carbonate and ferrous
sulfate. Milk as food is measurable but much smaller: in the
one study of it, taking levothyroxine with 355 mL of 2% cow milk lowered peak T4
and total exposure by about 8%. The review is explicit that the
separation needed for milk is unknown, and that the finding cannot be extended
to plant-based milks.

So dairy at breakfast, after the window, is not the thing to lose sleep over.
Dairy inside the window -- the carton on the way out the door -- is.

Source: Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements -- A Systematic Review.

Source: Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information, U.S. National Library of Medicine.

What makes it hard to catch is the lag. Nothing on the carton identifies
itself as an interaction, and the effect shows up a week or two later as
tiredness or dizziness -- by which point you are far more likely to blame your
thyroid, your job or your sleep than a drink you started buying last Monday.

If your mornings have changed and you cannot think why, the question worth
asking is not only "what am I taking?" but "what am I drinking, and
when?"

Does going back to sleep after your dose matter?

Asked often, and the honest starting point is that no study has tested
lying down versus staying up after a morning dose. What exists is
indirect, and it points reassuringly in one direction.

Levothyroxine is absorbed in the small intestine, and how fast the stomach
empties is one of the main things that limits it. That is the reason to suspect
that dozing off might slow things down. But the strongest evidence available is
about people who sleep for eight hours straight after their dose: those who take
it at bedtime.

In a randomised double-blind crossover trial, moving the dose from morning to
bedtime improved the numbers -- TSH fell by 1.25 mIU/L, free T4 rose by
0.07 ng/dL and total T3 by 6.5 ng/dL. If a full night's sleep after the tablet
produced better results than a morning dose, going back to bed for two hours is
unlikely to be the thing ruining your levels.

Source: Bolk N et al., Effects of evening vs morning levothyroxine intake: a randomized double-blind crossover trial, Arch Intern Med 2010;170(22). See also a later pragmatic crossover trial in older patients.

If your own levels are off and you cannot explain it, this is still worth
raising with your doctor -- but it is far down the list, well below coffee,
supplements and simply taking it at a different time each day.

What about oat, almond or soy milk?

Two different things decide the answer, and both are printed on the carton.

Added calcium. Plant milks are usually fortified, and many are
fortified to match or exceed cow's milk. Cow's milk carries roughly 450 mg of
calcium per 355 mL. Read the label and compare: if your oat milk is in the same
range, treat it the same way you would treat milk.

Soy is a separate issue. MedlinePlus names soybeans, alongside
walnuts and dietary fibre, as things that can affect how levothyroxine works for
you, and soy protein taken close to a dose has been reported to interfere with
absorption. So soy milk carries a reason for caution that almond milk does not,
independent of how much calcium was added to it.

Sources: Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information; Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements -- A Systematic Review, which states plainly that the cow's milk finding cannot be extrapolated to plant-based alternatives.

The practical version: check the calcium figure on your carton, be a little more
careful with soy than with the others, and keep whichever one you use after the
window rather than inside it.

What Thyrowise does about it

Thyrowise turns the wait into something you do not have to hold in your head.
When you mark the morning dose taken, it starts a countdown -- on the Lock Screen,
in a widget, and on the Apple Watch -- and when the window closes it tells you
coffee and breakfast are fine. The wait length is yours to set; it ships at 30
minutes.

It also keeps the dose-change log, so the next lab result arrives with the
context of what changed and when.

Related: what a normal TSH actually is, and why
your lab's range differs from the one you read online *
how to track symptoms so the appointment is
worth something *
how to choose a thyroid tracker app.

Get Thyrowise on the App Store

Free * iPhone and Apple Watch * no account, no server

Questions people also ask

Does black coffee count?

It counts as breaking the empty stomach, which is what the window is
protecting. Milk adds calcium on top of that.

What if I forget and eat straight away?

One morning is one morning; it is not a dose you have to make up or double.
What is worth doing is noting it, so that if a lab result comes back odd you can
see whether that week was unusual. Never change a dose yourself -- that is your
doctor's call.

Can I take it at bedtime instead?

Some people do, because the requirement is an empty stomach rather than a
particular hour, and the evening can be easier to keep clear than the morning.
Discuss the switch with your doctor first, and expect the next TSH to be the
thing that confirms it worked.

# Thyrowise Support -- Contact and Medical Sources
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/support/

Thyrowise

Support.

Email aykutaydmr@gmail.com.
One person reads it, and replies. Include your iOS version and what you were
doing -- it saves a round trip.

Common answers are on the FAQ page: pricing, Android,
Apple Watch, Apple Health, export, and what happens to your data.

Where our medical information comes from

Thyrowise states a small number of medical facts -- typical reference ranges, a
retest interval, how levothyroxine is absorbed. Every one of them comes from a
published source, and the app names the source next to the claim. The rule for
the project is blunt: a claim with no source does not ship.

Everything else the app shows you is a count of your own logs, presented as a
count.

The claims, and what backs them

Lab reference ranges

Thyrowise shows typical adult ranges of about 0.4-4.0 mIU/L for TSH,
0.8-1.8 ng/dL for free T4 and 2.3-4.2 pg/mL for free T3, and says throughout that
ranges are approximate and differ between laboratories.

Thyroid Function Tests -- American Thyroid Association

When TSH is rechecked

Thyrowise says TSH is usually rechecked about 6-12 weeks after a dose change,
and waits that long before showing what a dose change did.

Hypothyroidism and ATA Professional Guidelines -- American Thyroid Association

Levothyroxine timing and absorption

Thyrowise says levothyroxine is absorbed best on an empty stomach and offers a
30-60 minute wait before coffee or breakfast, and says to keep calcium, iron,
magnesium and antacids at least 4 hours away from a dose.

Levothyroxine -- MedlinePlus Drug Information -- U.S. National Library of Medicine

TPO antibodies and Hashimoto's

Thyrowise describes TPO antibodies as the marker associated with Hashimoto's
thyroiditis, usually measured once rather than tracked.

Hashimoto's Thyroiditis -- American Thyroid Association; Hashimoto's Disease -- NIDDK, National Institutes of Health

The symptom list

The symptoms Thyrowise offers as one-tap chips are the ones commonly associated
with an underactive thyroid and Hashimoto's.

Hypothyroidism -- American Thyroid Association; Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid) -- NIDDK

Total vs free T4 and T3

A total measures bound and free hormone together, so it shifts when binding
proteins change, while free measurements more accurately reflect how the thyroid
is working.

Thyroid Function Tests -- American Thyroid Association

Thyroglobulin antibodies

Logged without a built-in normal range, because this test is reported against
each laboratory's own cut-off. Antibodies help make the initial diagnosis, but
following their levels over time does not track how the thyroid is doing.

Antithyroglobulin antibody test -- MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine; ATA

Reverse T3

Thyrowise records a reverse T3 result if you have one, and says plainly that a
review of the literature does not support measuring it routinely in the care of
hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, and that most clinicians do not use it.

Clinical Thyroidology for the Public, Vol 12 Issue 1 -- American Thyroid Association

TI-RADS categories

Thyrowise stores the TI-RADS category written on your ultrasound report and
links to the body that publishes the system. It does not score your scan or
interpret the report itself.

ACR Thyroid Imaging Reporting & Data System (TI-RADS) -- American College of Radiology

Thyrowise is a tracking and reminder tool. It is not a medical device and does
not give medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Reference ranges are
approximate and vary between laboratories. Always follow your doctor's plan;
never change your dose based on the app.

# What Is a Normal TSH Level? Ranges, and Why Your Lab's Differs
URL: https://thyrowise.github.io/what-is-a-normal-tsh/

Thyrowise

What is a normal TSH, and why does your lab's range differ?

A typical adult range is about 0.4-4.0 mIU/L. But "typical" is
doing a lot of work in that sentence, and the number that matters for you is
probably narrower.

Typical adult ranges

| Test | Typical adult range | Units

| TSH | about 0.4 - 4.0 | mIU/L

| Free T4 | about 0.8 - 1.8 | ng/dL

| Free T3 | about 2.3 - 4.2 | pg/mL

Source: Thyroid Function Tests, American Thyroid Association. These ranges are approximate and vary between laboratories.

Why two labs disagree about the same blood

A reference range is not a law of nature. Each laboratory establishes its own
interval from its own assay and its own reference population, so the printed
range moves from lab to lab -- and can move again when a single lab changes
equipment.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly: compare your result
to the range printed on that result, not to a range you read somewhere
else. A value that looks marginally high against a stranger's range can sit
comfortably inside your own lab's.

"Normal" and "your target" are not the same thing

The printed range describes a population. The number your doctor is steering
you toward describes you -- and for someone on levothyroxine it is often narrower
than the full range, and sometimes deliberately offset from the middle of it.

Someone told to stay under 2.5 does not get useful information from an app that
colours everything below 4.0 green. That is why Thyrowise asks for
your band and draws the chart against that, instead of against a
generic normal.

TSH moves slowly, and that is the point

After a levothyroxine dose change, TSH is usually rechecked about
6 to 12 weeks later, because that is roughly how long it takes to
settle at the new dose.

Source: Hypothyroidism and ATA Professional Guidelines, American Thyroid Association.

This is why a single reading tells you so little on its own, and why a chart
with the dose changes marked on it tells you so much: the question is never
"what is my TSH", it is "what did my TSH do after the thing that changed".

Free versus total, and the tests that are not trend lines

Free T4 and free T3 measure unbound hormone. A
total counts bound and free together, so it shifts when
binding proteins change -- in pregnancy, for instance -- while the free
measurements more accurately reflect how the thyroid is working.
(ATA, Thyroid Function Tests)

TPO antibodies are the marker associated with Hashimoto's
thyroiditis. They are usually measured once, to answer a question, rather
than tracked over time.
(ATA; NIDDK)

Thyroglobulin antibodies are reported against each
laboratory's own cut-off rather than one shared number. They help make the
initial diagnosis, but following their level over time does not track how
the thyroid is doing.
(MedlinePlus)

Reverse T3 is not supported for routine use in the care of
hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, and most clinicians do not use it.
(ATA, Clinical Thyroidology for the Public 12(1))

What Thyrowise does about it

You enter the target band your doctor actually gave you, and the TSH chart is
drawn against that band with your dose changes marked on the same timeline. Every
value you log keeps its own date, so the shape of the last two years is one
screen rather than a folder of PDFs. Thyrowise stores results; it does not
interpret them or tell you what your dose should be.

Get Thyrowise on the App Store

Free * iPhone and Apple Watch * no account, no server

About this page

Written by the developer of Thyrowise. I am not a doctor and this is
not medical advice -- it is a plain-language write-up of published
guidance, with every claim linked to the source it came from so you can open it
and check.

Where it has been wrong, readers have caught it. The corrections on this page
came from people in r/Hypothyroidism
who knew the literature better than I did. If you find another,
tell me and I will fix it and say what changed.

Thyrowise is a tracking and reminder tool. It is not a medical device and does
not give medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Reference ranges are
approximate and vary between laboratories. Always follow your doctor's plan;
never change your dose based on the app.
